questions.q: According to the summary, why are TV remotes so confusing to use?
a: They pack in buttons to work with as many devices as possible
They are designed for engineers rather than families
They change their layout with every new model
They rely on touch screens that respond poorly
questions.why: Lesson 1 says makers cram remotes with options so they can connect to BluRay players, consoles and sound systems.

questions.q: Why do IKEA's different-sized nuts and bolts make assembly easier?
a: Each bolt fits only one matching hole, so mistakes are hard
The parts are labeled with numbers in the manual
Every bolt can go anywhere, which speeds things up
The pieces click together without any tools
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes this as a physical constraint: one correct place for each part guides the builder.

questions.q: What example of a cultural constraint does the summary give?
a: Screws tighten when turned right and loosen when turned left
Only one size of bolt fits each hole in a dresser
Programs remind you to save before closing a file
A dishwasher offers a single wash cycle
questions.why: Lesson 2 gives the near-universal screw direction as a cultural constraint we rarely notice.

questions.q: What is the first step in the human-centred design process described?
a: Watch real people use the product and record their problems
Build a prototype and test it in a lab
Brainstorm fixes before studying any users
Ask customers which features they want most
questions.why: Lesson 3 says you cannot judge a product without watching people use it, so observation comes first.

questions.q: According to the summary, what goes wrong when technology advances faster than design?
a: Products grow too complicated for consumers to use easily
Companies run out of ideas for new features
Users stop buying new devices altogether
Designers lose interest in solving human problems
questions.why: Lesson 1 warns that when a design becomes too complicated, it becomes useless to the consumer.
